why.support: Online shops want you to click fast. Some reviews are fake. Learn to tell **fact** from **opinion**. Learn your rights. Then you won't get ripped off.
why.core: Online shops are built to make you click fast. Reviews can be fake, and timers can be fake too. But a careful reader can tell a **fact** from an **opinion**, a useful review from an empty one, and a real shop from a dodgy one. And if something goes wrong, the law is on your side, as long as you know what it says.
why.extend: Online shopping is a persuasive environment: reviews, ratings, timers and pricing are all chosen to move you to buy. Evaluating that language (fact or opinion, substantiated or bare, independent or self-serving) is how you make a reliable decision. Knowing the law means you can act when something goes wrong.

articles.title: How to buy smart online

body.support:
Online shops want you to buy **fast**. Slow down.

**1. Check the shop.** Is there a real address and phone number? Search the shop's name with the word *scam*. Never pay by **bank transfer, gift card or crypto**.

**2. Read reviews like a detective.**

- *Best ever!!!* is an **opinion**. It doesn't help.
- *The battery lasted four hours* is a **fact**. It helps.

Read the 2- and 3-star reviews too. Fake reviews are against the law.

**3. Know your rights.** Is it **faulty**? You can get a **repair, replacement or refund**, even on sale. Just don't like it? The shop doesn't have to help.

**4. Buy Now Pay Later** means paying in parts. It's still **debt**.
body.core:
Online shops are built to make you buy, fast. Countdown timers, *only 3 left!*, and huge discounts all push you to click before you think. Slow down. Here's how to buy smart.

**1. Check the seller.** Is there a real address and phone number, not just an email? Search the shop's name with the words *reviews* or *scam*, and see what other sites say. Scamwatch warns that fake shops often sell popular items for far less than anywhere else. Their biggest giveaway is how they want you to pay: **bank transfer, gift cards or crypto**. That money is almost impossible to get back.

**2. Read reviews like a detective.** Reviews mix **facts** (things you could check) and **opinions** (what someone thinks or feels).

- *These are the best earbuds EVER!!!* is an opinion. It tells you nothing.
- *The battery lasted about four hours, not the eight it claims* is a fact. It's useful.

The most useful reviews give **details**. Read the 2- and 3-star reviews, not just the 5s. Be suspicious of lots of reviews with the same wording, or posted on the same day. Reviews on the shop's own site may be chosen by the shop. Fake reviews are illegal in Australia.

**3. Know your rights.** Under Australian Consumer Law, products must work, match their description, and do what the seller said. If something is **faulty**, you have the right to a **repair, replacement or refund**, even if it was on sale. A sign saying *No refunds* is unlawful. But if you just **change your mind**, the shop doesn't have to help. Buying from overseas? Getting your money back can be much harder.

**4. Think before Buy Now Pay Later.** BNPL lets you pay in parts. It's still **debt**, and late payments can cost you fees. Since June 2025, BNPL companies have needed a credit licence, like other lenders.
body.extend:
Online retail is designed to accelerate decisions. Countdown timers, scarcity claims (*only 3 left!*) and inflated *was* prices all apply pressure. Buying well means slowing down and evaluating what you read.

**1. Verify the seller.** Look for a physical address and phone number, then cross-check the business on independent sites. Scamwatch notes that fake stores often advertise popular items far below normal prices. The clearest warning sign is the payment method: **bank transfers, gift cards and cryptocurrency** are almost impossible to recover.

**2. Evaluate reviews.** Distinguish **facts** (verifiable) from **opinions** (judgements and feelings), and substantiated claims from bare assertions.

- *Best earbuds EVER!!!* asserts a judgement but offers no evidence.
- *The battery lasted about four hours, not the advertised eight* is specific and checkable.

Weight detailed reviews, read the mid-range ratings, and be wary of clusters with similar wording or dates. Consider the source: a shop's own site may select or edit what it displays. Fake reviews are illegal under Australian Consumer Law.

**3. Know your rights.** Consumer guarantees require goods to be of acceptable quality, match their description and be fit for purpose. **Faulty** goods entitle you to a **repair, replacement or refund**, including sale items, and blanket *No refunds* signs are unlawful. **Change of mind** isn't covered. Remedies from overseas sellers can be much harder to obtain.

**4. Treat Buy Now Pay Later as debt.** It splits a purchase into instalments, with late fees if you miss one. Since June 2025, providers have needed an Australian credit licence.

caseStudies.title: The reviews that weren't real

body.support:
**Service Seeking** is a website for finding tradies. Customers can leave reviews.

But there was a problem. Businesses could write reviews about **themselves**. The reviews looked like they came from **customers**.

The **ACCC** protects shoppers. It took Service Seeking to court.

In **2020**, the court said Service Seeking had to pay **$600,000**.

The lesson: you can't always trust reviews. Check more than one place.
body.core:
**Service Seeking** is an Australian website where people find tradies and other businesses for jobs. Customers could leave reviews of the businesses they used.

But the **ACCC**, the government agency that protects shoppers, found a problem. Through a feature called **Fast Feedback**, businesses could write reviews about their **own** work. Those reviews then appeared as if they'd been written by **customers**.

Thousands of reviews were published this way. People reading them had no way of knowing who really wrote them.

The ACCC took Service Seeking to court. Service Seeking admitted it had broken the law.

In **July 2020**, the Federal Court ordered it to pay a **$600,000** penalty. It also had to publish notices correcting what it had done, and set up a program to make sure it followed the law.

The lesson: a review is only as good as its **source**. If you can't tell who wrote it, check somewhere else too.
body.extend:
**Service Seeking** is an Australian website that connects customers with tradies and other businesses. It has a customer review system.

The **ACCC**, the national consumer regulator, took action over a feature called **Fast Feedback**. It let businesses publish reviews of their own work. Those reviews were presented as if customers had written them. Thousands were published this way, and readers had no way of knowing who really wrote them.

Service Seeking admitted it had broken the law. In **July 2020**, the Federal Court ordered it to pay a **$600,000** penalty. It also had to publish corrective notices and set up a compliance program.

The case shows that a review is only as reliable as its source. Reviews often look independent. But who selected, wrote or published them matters. Checking several independent sources is how you test a claim.

model.text:
**Should you buy the SoundPod earbuds from DealZone? No.**

I checked three things.

**The shop.** The website has no ABN, no phone number and no street address. These are warning signs of a fake shop.

**The reviews.** All 40 reviews have five stars. They were all posted in the same week. Real reviews are mixed.

**The price.** The earbuds cost $29 here. Three other shops sell them for $120 to $150.

My advice: buy them from a shop you can check, and pay with PayPal or a credit card.

teacher.overview: Students evaluate online shopping texts: product pages, ratings and reviews. They distinguish fact, opinion and feeling, and bare assertions from substantiated claims, and check sellers across independent sources. They learn their consumer guarantee rights (repair, replace or refund for faulty goods; no change-of-mind entitlement; 'No refunds' signs are unlawful) and that Buy Now Pay Later is debt. The case study is the ACCC's 2020 Federal Court case against Service Seeking over misleading reviews. The final task checks a real shop and writes a substantiated recommendation.

Check shopping sites and review sites are reachable on school devices.
Print the made-up product page if devices are limited.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** a fact can be checked; an opinion is what someone thinks or feels. Check for a real address and phone number; search the name with *reviews* or *scam* on other sites. Faulty: repair, replacement or refund.

**Product page:** 1 price (suspiciously low); 2 pressure (timer, scarcity); 3 rating (who wrote them?); 4 opinion (no details); 5 facts (specific, useful); 6 returns (unlawful if faulty); 7 payment (bank transfer: red flag).

**Sort:** strap broke — fact; best shoes — opinion; arrived in three days — fact; love love love — opinion; darker than the photo — fact; nice person — opinion.

**Case study:** businesses could write reviews of their own work that appeared to come from customers; the source decides how reliable a review is; independent review sites, Google reviews, forums, friends.

**Know your rights:** faulty — repair, replace or refund; change of mind — the shop doesn't have to help unless its policy says so; the sign is unlawful and you're still entitled to a remedy; BNPL is debt: can you make all four payments on time, and is it worth it?

realityCheck: **Students already shop online,** often through social media ads and marketplaces. Use their examples; they're more real than anything you'll prepare.
**BNPL is mostly for over-18s,** but students see it at every checkout and many will use it soon. ASIC's 2020 research found 21% of BNPL users surveyed had missed a payment in the previous 12 months.
**Rights can sound abstract.** A quick role-play (student returns faulty headphones; teacher is a difficult shop assistant) makes them stick.
**Some reviews are honestly mixed.** The goal isn't to distrust everything, but to weigh evidence.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's directly useful, and pairs well with Review It (writing reviews) and Spot the Scam.
